# Discussion and Future Directions

## Thesis Aims Review

The introduction set out five specific aims. Here I look back at each of them and how far I was able to accomplish it.

**Aim 1 — Confirm that proNGF increases axonal tau ** The main result of this thesis is that axonal treatment of proNGF increases total tau in BFCNs, most clearly in the soma. Across several independent experiments, proNGF raised total tau in the soma enough to be significant; the axon moved in the same direction but more variably and did not reach significance on its own. I believe this was partially due to the unsuitable use of actin as a loading control in the first experiments: especially in the axon, actin levels change when the axon is treated with proNGF, which makes those results unreliable, whereas the shifts in the soma were smaller (@fig-appkd-actin). 

**Aim 2 — Determine whether blocking APP synthesis prevents the tau increase, establishing whether APP and tau act in parallel or in a linear pathway.** APP is not upstream of tau, proNGF treatment raised tau even when siAPP was present (siAPP + proNGF was higher than siAPP in both compartments), which would argue against APP being required — but I did not confirm that the siAPP was working. An incomplete or failed knockdown would produce exactly the result I saw. Confirming that siAPP lowers APP is therefore the first thing that needs to be done before any conclusion about APP dependence can be drawn.

**Aim 3 — Quantify total and phosphorylated tau and identify phospho-tau species associated with degeneration.** Total tau was quantified, as described under Aim 1. The phospho-tau side was only in very initial steps: I used the most common phospho-tau antibodies available, against pSer202/pThr205 (AT8) and pThr181, and could not show any surplus of phospho-tau relative to total tau in response to treatment, so no specific degeneration-associated phospho-species was identified. This might be because I need to do more experiments, or because I need to look at other phospho-sites, or at additional post-translational modifications such as acetylation, which has been associated with tau pathology in traumatic brain injury [@shinReducingAcetylatedTau2021].

**Aim 4 — Measure total and isoform-specific tau mRNA after proNGF.** The ddPCR confirmed that tau mRNA is present in the axon and rises with proNGF, in the same direction as the protein, but a reliable quantitative and isoform-resolved measurement was not achieved because the reference gene was itself changed by the treatment. The details, and the planned fixes, are in the next section.

**Aim 5 — Use IPA to identify novel signaling pathways engaged after proNGF that contribute to degeneration.** IPA placed MAPT and APP among the most significant upstream regulators of the axonal nascent proteome — a result that held and grew stronger when I re-ran the analysis against the updated knowledge base — and it pointed to coordinated translational stress, cytoskeletal disruption, and suppression of pro-survival signaling, along with new regulators such as RYR1 and PSEN1. These analyses, and the mechanistic hypotheses that came out of them (IRES-mediated tau translation and a tau–14-3-3 interaction), are presented in the proteomics chapter.

## Tau mRNA (ddPCR) — follow-up and interpretation

The ddPCR experiment was aimed at asking whether the tau increase is reflected at the mRNA level and whether the isoform selectivity seen in the proteome (both 0N3R and 0N4R in the soma, only 0N3R newly synthesized in the axon) exists in the transcript pool. The experiment confirmed that tau mRNA is detectable in the axon compartment of filter chamber cultures and that the primers designed in the shared 5' UTR of *Mapt* amplify reliably from both compartments; and under control conditions the soma has substantially more tau mRNA than the axon, consistent with the cell body being the main site of transcript abundance and the axon holding a smaller, localized pool. The raw axon tau copies also rose about 10-fold after proNGF, in the same direction as the protein data.

The experiment could not, however, give a reliable quantitative answer, because of the control used. Actin changed dramatically with treatment and normalizing tau to actin therefore didn't produce valid results. There are two likely explanations: actin mRNA may itself be upregulated in axons after proNGF, as part of the cytoskeletal remodeling that accompanies growth and degeneration, which would make actin unusable as a reference here; or the amount of RNA loaded differed between the control and proNGF wells, so the actin difference reflects input rather than biology. Either way, without a valid reference gene or equalized input, the fold-change cannot be trusted.

The follow-ups that address this are: First, I will replace beta-actin with GAPDH, which is not a cytoskeletal protein and is less likely to respond to proNGF, giving a more stable baseline. Second, I will run the experiment in parallel in filter chambers and in whole-cell well cultures: because the axon contributes very little material, the whole-lysate signal should be dominated by the soma, and agreement between the whole-cell and soma measurements would give confidence that the compartmental values are reliable. Third, we are ordering primers specific to the 0N3R and 0N4R transcripts rather than the shared 5' UTR, so that the isoform selectivity observed at the protein level — only 0N3R newly synthesized in the axon — can be tested directly at the mRNA level in each compartment. Together these should turn the current qualitative observation (tau mRNA is present in axons and rises with proNGF) into a quantitative, isoform-resolved measurement.

## Does proNGF disrupt the axon initial segment?

One surprise from the results is that tau accumulates most clearly in the soma, even though the mass-spectrometry data point to the axon as the main site of newly synthesized tau after proNGF. New synthesis in the axon is one way to raise somatic tau, but it is not the only one: tau could also be redistributed from the axon back into the soma. A mechanism that can be the cause for this kind of redistribution can be the axon initial segment (AIS).

The AIS contains a "tau diffusion barrier" that normally keeps tau in the axon by limiting its retrograde (axon-to-soma) movement, and this barrier depends on an intact AIS cytoskeleton — ankyrin-G, EB1, and dynamic AIS microtubules [@zempelAxodendriticSortingPathological2017]. When the AIS is disturbed, the barrier fails and axonal tau missorts into the somatodendritic compartment; this is also one of the early events in Alzheimer's disease [@zempelAxodendriticSortingPathological2017]. Neuronal injury also causes rapid, calpain-mediated breakdown of the AIS cytoskeleton (loss of ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin), independent of cell death or axon degeneration [@schaferDisruptionAxonInitial2009].

This suggests an explanation for the somatic tau increase I see: proNGF, acting on the axon through p75NTR, drives axonal stress and degeneration — I showed here that it activates JNK, and its degenerative effect on BFCN axons is well established — and this could compromise the AIS and its tau diffusion barrier. If the barrier weakens, tau that would normally be held in the axon could leak retrogradely into the soma, adding to the somatic signal measured by Western blot even without a change in the total amount of tau made. In this view the soma accumulation would be partly a sorting failure and not only new synthesis, and the two mechanisms are not mutually exclusive.

To test this hypothesis we can use the same approach as @schaferDisruptionAxonInitial2009. The AIS can be visualized by immunostaining for ankyrin-G, βIV-spectrin, or TRIM46, and its length and integrity compared between control and proNGF axons — a shortened, fragmented, or lost AIS after proNGF would be the first prediction. If AIS disruption correlates with somatic tau, the next step is to block it — for example with calpain inhibition, which preserves the AIS cytoskeleton after injury [@schaferDisruptionAxonInitial2009], or GSK3 inhibition — and ask whether protecting the AIS reduces the proNGF-induced rise in somatic tau.

## Do specific isoforms of Tau play a role in axon degeneration in response to p75NTR signaling?

The proteomics showed that the tau newly synthesized in the axon is specifically the 0N3R isoform, which raises the question of whether this particular isoform is functionally involved in the degeneration signal that p75NTR triggers, rather than tau in general.

Tau isoforms differ by whether exon 10 is included: exon 10 encodes the second of the four microtubule-binding repeats, so its inclusion produces 4R tau and its exclusion produces 3R tau. To knock down the 3R isoforms specifically — the group that includes the axonal 0N3R — a siRNA was designed and ordered against the splice junction where exon 9 joins directly to exon 11. That junction exists only in transcripts that have skipped exon 10, so the siRNA marks 3R tau mRNA for degradation while leaving 4R tau untouched.

The plan is to apply this siRNA in the compartmental (filter- and microfluidic-chamber) cultures, treat the axons with proNGF, and ask whether removing the axonal 3R tau changes the degeneration outcome — axon fragmentation and neuronal death — compared with a non-targeting control siRNA. Two controls are important: confirming by blot or PCR that the siRNA lowers 3R tau without lowering 4R tau, and confirming that it acts in the axon compartment. If 0N3R tau is part of how the retrograde death signal is executed — for example by supporting the dynein–dynactin transport that carries the signal back to the soma, given that blocking retrograde transport with ciliobrevin D was already shown to prevent proNGF-induced degeneration [@dasguptaProNGFElicitsRetrograde2024] — then knocking it down should protect the axons. If degeneration proceeds unchanged, the 0N3R increase would instead be a bystander of the response rather than a driver.

## Where does the newly synthesized tau end up?

If proNGF drives tau synthesis in the axon, the next question is what that new tau actually does — where it goes and what it binds. There are a few possibilities, and each is a hypothesis that can be tested:

- **On microtubules, doing its normal job.** The simplest option is that the new tau binds axonal microtubules and stabilizes them. This can be tested with a microtubule co-sedimentation assay — spinning down taxol-stabilized microtubules from axon lysates and measuring how much tau pellets with them, in control versus proNGF.

- **Riding with, or modulating, the p75NTR signaling endosome.** proNGF is internalized with p75NTR and carried retrogradely to the soma as a death signal [@dasguptaProNGFElicitsRetrograde2024]. Because tau regulates motor-driven transport along microtubules, the new tau could travel with this retrograde endosome or change how fast it moves. This can be tested by co-immunoprecipitating tau and blotting for p75NTR, and by live imaging of labeled p75 endosomes with and without tau knockdown to see whether their retrograde movement changes.

- **Controlling mitochondrial transport.** Tau bound to microtubules can slow or stall mitochondrial movement. If new tau builds up on axonal microtubules, it could stall mitochondria at the site of proNGF signaling, which would fit a local stress and degeneration response. This can be tested by live imaging of mitochondria (MitoTracker) in the axon, measuring transport speed and flux in control versus proNGF, with and without tau knockdown.

- **Sequestering 14-3-3 (YWHAZ) and releasing an apoptotic signal.** 14-3-3ζ (YWHAZ) — which came up in the proteomics (@fig-ywhaz-abundance) — normally holds pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bad inactive. Tau binds 14-3-3, so a rise in tau could tie up 14-3-3ζ and free Bad, linking the tau increase directly to the death pathway. This can be tested by co-immunoprecipitating tau and blotting for 14-3-3ζ, and asking whether more tau after proNGF is accompanied by more free (unbound) Bad.

The most general way to address all of these at once is to isolate the newly synthesized tau specifically and identify its partners. Nascent protein can be metabolically labeled — for example with puromycin or the methionine analog AHA — and tau, or the labeled nascent fraction, pulled down and analyzed by mass spectrometry or by targeted Western blots for the candidates above. This co-immunoprecipitation of nascent tau, and asking what comes down with it, would turn the list of hypotheses into a single experiment that says which partners the new tau actually engages after proNGF.
